humanities_role_explanation: The benchmark uses humanities topics (such as history, philosophy, world religions, and music) purely as content sources to generate open-ended factual prompts. Disciplinary competence is not evaluated; instead, the evaluation framework (SAFE) verifies isolated atomic facts against Google Search results, treating humanities material as raw declarative data rather than an object of interpretive, aesthetic, or historical reasoning.
benchmark_modalities_explanation: A text-only prompt dataset (LongFact) and text-based evaluation pipeline (SAFE) utilizing web-search text snippets.
analytical_tasks_explanation: The benchmark tests open-ended question answering (open_ended_qa) and long-form text generation (generation). The evaluator (SAFE) employs LLM agents for information extraction (breaking text down into self-contained atomic facts), agentic tool use (generating search queries dynamically), and fact verification (confirming if extracted claims are supported by search results).

general_purpose_benchmark.note: Evaluates LLM factuality across 38 diverse academic and general topics including STEM, social sciences, and the humanities.

evaluates_generative_llm.note: Evaluates 13 prominent generative LLMs across Gemini, GPT, Claude, and PaLM-2 model families.

quantitative_metrics.note: Uses precision, recall (R_K), and F1@K metrics to measure long-form factuality.

published_after_march_2023.note: Published at NeurIPS 2024; first preprint released in March 2024.

summary: The paper introduces LongFact, a prompt set of 2,280 questions across 38 topics designed to evaluate the factuality of LLMs in generating long-form, multi-paragraph responses. To automate the highly expensive process of human evaluation, it proposes the Search-Augmented Factuality Evaluator (SAFE), which utilizes an LLM agent to decompose responses into atomic facts and verify them through iterative Google Search queries. The authors also propose the F1@K metric, balancing factual precision with length-preferred recall, to provide a standardized score for long-form factual performance.
key_findings: Larger language models generally exhibit better long-form factuality, with GPT-4-Turbo, Gemini-Ultra, and PaLM-2-L-IT-RLHF performing best. The automated evaluator SAFE agrees with crowdsourced human annotators 72% of the time, wins 76% of disagreement cases, and is over 20 times more cost-effective ($0.19 vs. $4.00 per response).
facets_explanation: The benchmark relies on an automated LLM-agent framework (SAFE) to generate factual annotations dynamically using Google Search (model_generated). Answering the prompts successfully requires external knowledge not supplied in the query (gold_beyond_stimulus). Disagreements between human crowdsourced annotators and the automated rater were treated as errors/noise to be resolved by expert adjudication (noise).
results_explanation: The best-performing model on the benchmark is GPT-4-Turbo, which achieves a headline F1@64 score of 95.0% as shown in Table 2 (under 'GPT-4-Turbo' for 'F1@64'). No human baseline score is reported for the LongFact prompts, so human_baseline_reported is set to 'no'. The paper does not report any performance differences across distinct answer formats for evaluated models on the same data, nor does it evaluate or report on cultural asymmetries.
